title: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves

marking_points.text: Names visible light as the region between infrared and ultraviolet.
States that visible-light waves are transverse.

option_feedback.A: Polarisation restricts oscillation direction, not propagation direction.
option_feedback.B: Correct. The oscillations are confined to one transverse direction.
option_feedback.C: A frequency change is not the meaning of polarisation.
option_feedback.D: Oscillations parallel to travel describe a longitudinal wave.

marking_points.text: Selects option B.

option_feedback.A: Correct. Energy travels east even though oscillation is vertical.
option_feedback.D: The oscillation reverses, not the energy-transfer direction.

marking_points.text: Selects option A.

option_feedback.C: Correct. Their oscillations lie along the propagation direction, leaving no transverse direction to select.
option_feedback.D: Wave speed does not decide whether plane polarisation is possible.

marking_points.text: Selects option C.

parts.answer: Energy is transferred horizontally towards the detector. The oscillation is vertical.

marking_points.text: States that energy transfer is horizontal towards the detector.
States that the oscillation direction is vertical.

parts.answer: Draw a vertical transmission axis. It is aligned with the wave's vertical oscillation direction.
accepted_alternatives: Vertical line through the filter with alignment explanation.

marking_points.text: Draws a vertical transmission axis on the filter.
Explains that the axis is aligned with the vertical oscillation direction.

parts.answer: The filter restricts the transverse oscillations to one direction perpendicular to propagation.
accepted_alternatives: The transmitted oscillations are confined to a single transverse direction or plane.

marking_points.text: States that the filter restricts the oscillation direction.
States that the selected direction is perpendicular to propagation.

parts.answer: Only a transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to travel with different transverse directions available. A rotated filter selects different components of those oscillations, so the changing received signal shows that transverse oscillations are present.

marking_points.text: States that a transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to its direction of travel.
Explains that rotating the filter changes which transverse oscillation direction or component is selected.
Concludes that the rotation-dependent signal is evidence that the wave is transverse.

parts.answer: Show the light oscillation perpendicular to the left-to-right travel direction, for example vertical. Show the sound-particle motion parallel to travel, left and right.
accepted_alternatives: Any light oscillation perpendicular to travel and sound motion parallel to travel.

marking_points.text: Adds a light oscillation arrow perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Adds sound-particle motion arrows parallel to the direction of travel.

parts.answer: A transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. The shown light oscillation is perpendicular to left-to-right energy transfer, so the light is transverse.
accepted_alternatives: Exact accepted definition followed by a correct application.

marking_points.text: States the accepted definition: a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Applies the perpendicular relationship to classify the light wave as transverse.

parts.answer: For light, rotation changes the selected transverse oscillation direction and can change transmission. For sound in air, particle motion is parallel to travel, so rotation cannot select a transverse oscillation direction and it cannot be plane polarised in this sense.
accepted_alternatives: Correct comparison of transverse light with longitudinal sound.

marking_points.text: Explains that rotating the filter changes the transverse oscillation direction selected from the light wave.
Explains that sound motion is parallel to travel, so no transverse direction can be selected and sound cannot be plane polarised in this sense.
